passage: "Three weeks, tops," said Xin, the lead developer, leaning back. The clinic's booking system in Durban had to move to new servers, and Lindiwe had to give the board a date by Friday. Three weeks already sounded like a fact. That evening she wrote at the top of a page: If nobody had said three, what would I guess? She didn't fully trust her answer, so she gathered comparisons. The pharmacy team's move last year took seven weeks. A friend at another clinic said theirs took six. The vendor's own case notes said five to eight. On Friday she told the board six to eight weeks and explained where each number came from. Xin grumbled, then admitted, "I was thinking of the easy part."

qa.q: How long did the pharmacy team's move take last year?
qa.a: Seven weeks.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe not trust her own first guess?
qa.a: She felt uneasy that Xin's three weeks was already sitting in her head like a fact, so she wanted numbers that did not start from it.

qa.q: What makes Lindiwe's method worth copying?
qa.a: She asked what she would judge without the first figure, then checked three separate sources before giving the board a range.

qa.q: How does Xin react to the six-to-eight-week estimate?
qa.a: Xin grumbles at first but then admits the three weeks only covered the easy part.

grounding: A young manager asks what she would estimate without the first figure and gathers three separate comparisons before deciding.

passage: At the community centre office, the caterer tapped his notebook. "For a health camp like this, you'll need three hundred plates." Kavitha, the new coordinator, nearly wrote 300 on the order form. Then she stopped and turned the form over. "Give me until four o'clock," she said. She asked herself what she would order if nobody had said three hundred. Then she looked for her own numbers. The registration sheet showed 140 names. Last year's camp register showed 170 people had come. And Tenzin, who ran the camp in the next ward, said they had fed about 150 with a few extra. At four she rang the caterer. "One eighty, please." Tenzin grinned when she told him. "Last year someone ordered three hundred. We ate rice for a week."

qa.q: How many names were on the registration sheet?
qa.a: The registration sheet showed 140 names.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha turn the order form over?
qa.a: She felt wary that the caterer's three hundred was about to become her number without any checking, so she wanted to think without it in front of her.

qa.q: Which sources did Kavitha use, and why does using several help?
qa.a: The registration sheet, last year's register and Tenzin's camp; separate figures that agree near 150 to 170 are safer than one opening number.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear her final order?
qa.a: Tenzin seems amused and pleased, remembering the year someone ordered three hundred and they ate rice for a week.

grounding: A coordinator sets aside a caterer's first figure and checks three independent numbers before placing the order.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,
You asked how the new job is going. Mostly well! One small thing from this week I want to tell you about. I had to score the interns' final reports, and my senior had already scribbled 4/10 on the corner of Rafiq's. The moment I saw it, everything I read looked like a four. So I stopped, covered the corner with a sticky note, and asked myself what I would give it if I had never seen that number. Then I put it next to two other reports I had already marked, and read the rubric again, line by line. It came out a seven, honestly, because his data section was the best of the three. I wrote a short note explaining why and gave it to my senior. She read it and changed hers to a six.
Miss you. Come to Pune soon.
Sunaina

qa.q: What score had the senior written on Rafiq's report?
qa.a: 4/10, scribbled on the corner.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina cover the corner with a sticky note?
qa.a: Sunaina felt uneasy that the four was colouring everything read afterwards, and wanted to judge the report fairly without it.

qa.q: What steps helped Sunaina reset the score?
qa.a: Asking what score it would get without the four, comparing it with two already-marked reports, and rereading the rubric line by line.

qa.q: How might Rafiq be affected by Sunaina's re-check?
qa.a: Rafiq's strong data section gets fair credit instead of being judged against a quick first mark.

grounding: A young worker hides a senior's first score, asks what the report deserves on its own and compares it with other marked reports.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today at lunch Dilnaz told us her cousin in Bhopal got bitten by a street dog and had to go to the hospital again and again. She said the dog came out of nowhere, growling, with its teeth showing. I could not eat my paratha after that.
On the way home, Bruno from the second floor wagged at me like always. I ran up the stairs so fast I dropped my water bottle. Mummy asked why. I said ALL dogs bite, Dilnaz said so. Mummy said Bruno has lived here six years and never bitten anyone. I said he just hasn't YET.
I am never going near any dog again. Not even Bruno.
Sarita

qa.q: What did Sarita drop while running up the stairs?
qa.a: Sarita dropped the water bottle.

qa.q: Why is Sarita so sure all dogs bite?
qa.a: Sarita feels scared, because Dilnaz's story was so vivid that one bite now seems like what every dog does, even Bruno.

qa.q: How could Mummy help Sarita feel safer around Bruno?
qa.a: She could stand with Sarita and watch Bruno from a little distance, talk about the gentle dogs they know, and show calm ways to be near a dog.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had told a story about a friendly dog instead?
qa.a: Sarita would probably remember that story most and greet Bruno as usual; the vivid story, not what dogs usually do, is steering the fear.

grounding: A child's diary shows one vivid dog-bite story turning into a belief that all dogs bite, even a familiar gentle one.

passage: The path to the gurdwara school ran past the Sandhus' farm, where old Moti lay in the shade every morning. For two years Baljeet had walked past him. Then on Sunday, at the tubewell, cousin Preeti told everyone how a dog in the next village had bitten a boy on the leg, how he screamed, how there was blood on his kurta. That night Baljeet dreamt of teeth. On Monday he stopped dead at the farm gate. "I'm going the long way," he said, and walked twenty minutes round the sugarcane, arriving late with muddy chappals. When his Bebe asked why, he said, "Dogs bite. Preeti said." "Which dogs?" "All of them." Moti, meanwhile, had not even lifted his head.

qa.q: Where did Moti lie every morning?
qa.a: In the shade at the Sandhus' farm.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet choose the long way round?
qa.a: He felt frightened because Preeti's story of the bitten boy was so vivid that it seemed any dog, even old Moti, might bite.

qa.q: What small step could help Baljeet?
qa.a: An adult could walk the old path with him, point out that Moti has lain there calmly for two years, and show him how to pass dogs calmly.

qa.q: What would change if Preeti had also talked about the many village dogs that never bite?
qa.a: Baljeet might see the bite as rare rather than normal, and keep walking his usual path past Moti.

grounding: After one vivid bite story, a boy decides all dogs bite and avoids a calm farm dog he has passed for two years.

passage: Clara's birthday invitation had a puppy on it, because Clara had a real one now, a fluffy beagle called Pip. Sofia put the card face down on her desk in their Madrid flat. At dinner on Sunday her uncle had told the story of a neighbour's dog that bit a delivery man, with a hand wrapped in bandages and a trip to hospital. Sofia had heard it once, but she kept seeing the bandages. "I can't go," she told her mother. "Clara's dog will bite." "Pip is ten weeks old," said her mother. "He mostly sleeps." "That's what everyone thinks. Then they bite." Her mother sat down beside her. "How many dogs do you know, Sofia?" Sofia counted: Pip, the baker's dog, Grandma's old Luna. None of them had ever bitten anyone.

qa.q: What is the name of Clara's puppy?
qa.a: Pip, a fluffy beagle.

qa.q: Why does Sofia feel sure Pip will bite?
qa.a: She feels scared because her uncle's bite story, with its bandages, keeps playing in her mind, so one case feels like what all dogs do.

qa.q: Why is her mother's question a good step?
qa.a: Counting the dogs Sofia really knows shows that none of them has bitten anyone, which balances the single scary story.

qa.q: How might Clara feel if Sofia skipped the party because of Pip?
qa.a: Clara would likely be disappointed and confused that her friend stayed away because of a sleepy puppy.

grounding: One vivid bite story at dinner makes a girl sure all dogs bite, until she counts the gentle dogs she actually knows.

passage: Ojas, sit. Before you say no to the Shimla trip, let your Irfan chacha tell you about Rukhsar. Last year, at fifteen, your cousin decided trains were death boxes. Her phone kept playing her crash clips, one after another: a derailment, a bus off a hill, a broken bridge. She watched them at night with the light off. When the school trip to Jaipur came, she tore up the form. "Abbu, it happens every day," she said. So I asked her one thing: "How many train journeys does our family make each week?" She counted. Her mother, me, her Dadi, the neighbours. Hundreds of journeys, and not one accident she could name except on her screen. She went on the trip in the end. She still grips the seat, but she went.

qa.q: What did Rukhsar do with the school trip form?
qa.a: She tore it up.

qa.q: Why did trains feel so dangerous to Rukhsar?
qa.a: She felt frightened because her phone kept playing crash clips at night, so accidents seemed to happen every day.

qa.q: What turning point changed Rukhsar's mind, and why did it work?
qa.a: Her father asking how many train journeys the family makes each week; counting real trips with no accident set the clips against her own life.

qa.q: How might Irfan have felt when Rukhsar tore up the form?
qa.a: He was likely worried for her and a bit sad that fear from clips was taking a trip away, which is why he asked a gentle question instead of scolding.

grounding: An uncle recalls how a teenage girl, fed a stream of crash clips, believed train travel was far riskier than her family's real journeys showed.

passage: Mummy's message came at 4:10: "Stuck at the bank till seven. Take the 312 bus to coaching, beta." Jyoti stared at the phone. The class started at five, and there was no one else to drop her. Her feed that week had been all dashcam clips: a bus jumping a red light in some city, a scooter skidding, a crowd around a crash. She had watched maybe forty of them. In her head, the 312 was a moving disaster. She called her mother. "Mummy, buses crash every day. I saw." "Where did you see?" "Online. Loads." Minakshi was quiet for a second. "Jyoti, how many times have you taken the 312?" "Maybe two hundred." "And?" Jyoti looked at the clock, grabbed her bag, and ran for the stop, still gripping her phone.

qa.q: What time did the class start?
qa.a: The class started at five.

qa.q: Why did the 312 bus feel like a disaster to Jyoti?
qa.a: She felt anxious because she had watched about forty crash clips that week, so accidents seemed far more common than in her own two hundred rides.

qa.q: What could Jyoti try when her feed fills up with crash clips?
qa.a: She could stop the stream and compare it with her own record, like two hundred safe rides on the 312, before judging how risky a trip is.

qa.q: What is it like for Minakshi to get this call while stuck at the bank?
qa.a: Minakshi is probably worried and short of time, but she stays calm and asks a question that helps Jyoti look at her own experience.

grounding: A teenager who has watched dozens of crash clips believes her everyday bus is a disaster, until asked how often she has ridden it safely.

passage: Uday used to cycle to school through the colony lanes of Lajpat Nagar. Now the cycle stood behind the washing machine with flat tyres. "Delhi roads are a death trap," he told his elder brother Ujjwal on Saturday, holding up his phone. "Watch this. And this one. Some guy flying off his bike." Ujjwal leaned over. The clips came from four different states, and one was from another country. "Where are these even from?" Uday shrugged. "Doesn't matter. It keeps happening." "Uday, you've watched twenty crashes this morning. How many have you seen with your own eyes in our lane?" Uday scrolled, frowning. "None. But that's because I stopped cycling." Ujjwal laughed, then pumped up the tyres anyway, just in case.

qa.q: Where did the cycle stand now?
qa.a: Behind the washing machine, with flat tyres.

qa.q: Why does Uday feel the roads are a death trap?
qa.a: He feels scared because his phone keeps showing crash after crash, and seeing them so often makes them seem common in his own lanes.

qa.q: What could help Uday judge his real risk?
qa.a: Checking where the clips come from, thinking about what he has actually seen in his lane, and perhaps riding with Ujjwal first to rebuild confidence.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see his brother's fear?
qa.a: Ujjwal finds it a bit funny but cares, noticing the clips come from all over and quietly pumping up the tyres in case Uday wants to ride.

grounding: A teenage boy watching crash clips from many places decides his own city roads are a death trap and stops cycling.

passage:
Tuesday. The news was wall to wall with the plane crash: the wreckage, the families, the black box. Sumit cancelled his flight to Kolkata for the internship and booked a thirty-hour train instead. "Flying is madness," he told Gopika in the canteen.
Thursday. He rode his scooter to the station to buy a printed ticket, his helmet hanging from the handle as always, weaving through market traffic. Gopika, on the back in her own helmet, tapped his shoulder. "You're scared of a plane but not of this?" "This is normal," he said.
Sunday. Gopika sent him a short article from the city traffic police about riders without helmets on their own roads. He read it at the station, then read it again. On Monday the helmet was on his head, and the train ticket stayed booked.

qa.q: How long was the train journey Sumit booked?
qa.a: It was a thirty-hour train.

qa.q: Why did flying feel like madness to Sumit?
qa.a: He felt frightened after days of dramatic crash coverage, so a rare danger felt huge while riding without a helmet felt normal and safe.

qa.q: What helped Sumit look at an everyday risk?
qa.a: Gopika's question and the traffic police article about riders on their own roads turned his attention to the danger he met daily, and he started wearing the helmet.

qa.q: What is it like for Gopika to ride pillion with Sumit?
qa.a: She is probably uneasy and a bit exasperated, since he fears planes but weaves through traffic with his helmet on the handle.

grounding: Over a week, a student who fears flying after crash coverage rides his scooter without a helmet until a friend points to the everyday risk.

passage: Sangeeta, you're worrying about that new virus in the news, na? Let me tell you your Vinita masi's old story. When I was twenty, the papers were full of a strange fever in some faraway district. Every morning there was a new photo of a hospital ward. I stopped eating street food, I washed my hands until they cracked, I even skipped my best friend's wedding because it would be crowded. And every single day of that year I rode my scooter to college without a helmet, hair flying, because helmets spoiled my hair. The fever never came near our town. What did happen was a skid on the wet road outside the bus stand. I got up with a torn elbow and a dented scooter. Only then did I buy a helmet.

qa.q: Why did Vinita ride without a helmet at twenty?
qa.a: Because helmets spoiled Vinita's hair.

qa.q: What was young Vinita feeling during the year of the fever news?
qa.a: She felt frightened of the fever because of the daily ward photos, yet felt safe on the scooter because riding was so ordinary.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Vinita's habit, and what might have come sooner?
qa.a: The skid outside the bus stand made her buy a helmet; asking which danger she met every single day could have led her there before the fall.

qa.q: How might Vinita's best friend have felt when Vinita skipped the wedding?
qa.a: The friend was likely hurt and puzzled that Vinita stayed away from a happy day because of a fever in a faraway district.

grounding: An aunt recalls fearing a rare fever from the news at twenty while riding without a helmet every day, until a skid.

passage: Exam day, 8:40 a.m., and the auto hadn't come. Uma had twenty minutes to reach the far campus. "Take my scooter," said Noor, tossing the keys. "The helmet's cracked, just go without." Uma was on the seat before Noor finished. This was the same Uma who had stopped using the college pool three weeks ago, after a news channel ran a whole evening on a rare infection from lake water two states away. She had read every article since. She had lectured Noor about the pool water twice. Now she was pulling into morning traffic bareheaded without a second thought. At the gate, Noor ran after her. "Wait! Take the warden's spare helmet!" Uma stopped, took it, strapped it on, and only then noticed how fast her heart was going.

qa.q: Why did Uma stop using the college pool?
qa.a: A news channel ran a whole evening on a rare infection from lake water two states away.

qa.q: Why did Uma not think twice about riding without a helmet?
qa.a: She was anxious about the exam and the scooter felt ordinary, while the rare infection from the news felt vivid and frightening, so the everyday danger didn't register.

qa.q: What protective step happens, and what could Uma ask herself next time?
qa.a: Noor brings the warden's spare helmet; next time Uma could ask which risk she actually meets each day before deciding what to fear.

qa.q: How might Noor see Uma's fears after this morning?
qa.a: Noor may find it strange and a bit worrying that Uma avoids a pool over one rare story yet nearly rode off without a helmet.

grounding: A student avoids the pool after coverage of a rare infection but almost rides a scooter without a helmet under exam pressure.

passage: The parents' meeting at the playschool had barely started when Parul's mother-in-law held up her phone. "Children are being taken from outside schools! It's on the family group. A white van." Three grandmothers gasped. Someone asked about extra guards. Tenzin, holding his eight-month-old son on his knee, read the forward. No date, no place, no name. He had seen the same message last year, with a different colour van. Then he glanced at the play corner: a plug socket without a cover, a heavy shelf not fixed to the wall, a bucket of mop water by the door. "Could we ask the police station what has actually been reported here?" he said. "And maybe fix that shelf today?" The room went quiet. The head teacher wrote both down.

qa.q: What dangers did Tenzin notice in the play corner?
qa.a: A plug socket without a cover, a heavy shelf not fixed to the wall, and a bucket of mop water by the door.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's reading of the forward suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and calm rather than panicked, noticing the message had no date or place and had gone round before, while real dangers sat in the play corner.

qa.q: Why are Tenzin's two requests sensible?
qa.a: Asking the police station what has actually been reported checks the rumour, and fixing the shelf deals with a risk that is really in the room.

qa.q: How might Parul's mother-in-law feel when the room goes quiet?
qa.a: She may feel a little embarrassed but also relieved that someone is checking, since her worry came from real love for the children.

grounding: A new father watches relatives panic over a forwarded kidnapping rumour, notices real hazards in the room and asks what has actually been reported.

passage:
Dear Usha akka,
Since you asked how the first months with baby Mihir are going: tiring, happy, and full of forwards. This week Amma's side of the family went into full panic over a message saying strangers in a grey van were taking babies from our district. Periamma called three times. Appa wanted to stop the nanny taking Mihir out in the pram. I checked with a friend at the district police office: there hasn't been a single case here this year. Meanwhile, the same relatives who were panicking keep leaving pills on the low table and hot tea on the edge of the bed where Mihir rolls. I said so, as gently as I could, and asked everyone to keep those up high. Amma sulked, then moved the tea.
Naveen, your very tired brother

qa.q: What did Naveen's friend at the district police office say?
qa.a: That there hasn't been a single case in the district this year.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel about the family's panic?
qa.a: He seems tired and a little frustrated, but steady, because the rumour had no local cases while real dangers sat on the low table.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that helped, and how did he do it?
qa.a: He checked the facts with the police office and gently asked everyone to keep pills and tea up high, turning worry toward the real risks.

qa.q: How might Amma feel after being told about the tea?
qa.a: Amma probably felt a bit hurt and sulked, but she moved the tea, showing she cares about Mihir's safety.

grounding: A new father sees relatives panic over a forwarded rumour, checks the local facts and points to the everyday risks at home.

passage: Damini, you asked what being a new dad is like. Honestly? It's mostly managing the family group. Last month someone forwarded a video of a masked man grabbing a child from a park, with "Happening in our city NOW" in red letters. By evening my mother had cancelled Esther's park walks, my aunt wanted a tracker in her booties, and my cousin called me careless for opening a window. I watched the video properly. The signs in it were in another language, and the same clip had been fact-checked two years ago. So I did the boring thing: I asked our local ward office how many children had gone missing in our area. Answer: none this year. What they did mention was falls from balconies. We have a balcony. Francis, the fun dad, spent Sunday putting up a grille.

qa.q: What did the ward office mention instead?
qa.a: Falls from balconies.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling while the family panicked?
qa.a: He felt doubtful and a bit worn out by the panic, but steady enough to check the video and ask the ward office for real numbers.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking the ward office how many children had actually gone missing, which replaced a scary clip with local facts and pointed him to the balcony.

qa.q: How might Francis's mother see the park walks now?
qa.a: She may still feel nervous after the video, but the local facts give her a reason to let Esther go back to the park.

grounding: A new father tells how relatives panicked over a forwarded clip while he checked the local figures and found the real risk at home.

passage: The trek company needed a yes or no by midnight, and at 9 p.m. Swati was still telling the story: a trekker lost for three days on the same trail, the search helicopter, the frozen fingers. Afreen felt her stomach tighten. She had her cancel email typed. Then she stopped. "Hang on. How often does that actually happen?" Swati shrugged. "It was all over the news." "That's why I remember it." Afreen spent the next hour on the forest department's trail page and the trek company's safety records. Thousands of people walked that route every season; the rare emergencies were mostly solo walkers off the marked path. At 11:40 she replied yes, asking to stay with the registered group and the guide. Then she deleted the cancel email.

qa.q: What deadline did the trek company set?
qa.a: A yes or no by midnight.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as Swati told the story?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with her stomach tightening, enough to type a cancel email before stopping to ask how common the danger really was.

qa.q: What steps did Afreen take before deciding, and why do they help?
qa.a: She checked the forest department's trail page and the company's safety records, then chose to stay with the registered group, so her choice rests on real figures rather than one vivid story.

qa.q: How might Swati see Afreen's final decision?
qa.a: Swati may be surprised, since the news story felt convincing, but might also learn something from the way Afreen checked.

grounding: Under a midnight deadline, a young woman pauses over a vivid trekking story, checks reliable records and then decides.

passage: Noor's voice note was dramatic: a lift in a Thane tower had dropped two floors with six people inside, screaming, doors jammed. By the time Jahnavi reached her own building in Andheri, she was eyeing the lift like an animal. Eleven floors of stairs with a laptop bag? She actually put her foot on the first step. Then she sat down on it. The story was vivid, but how often did lifts fail like that? She checked the certificate framed beside the lift door: inspected last month. She asked the watchman how long the lift had run. Twelve years, he said, two breakdowns, both just stuck, nobody hurt. She read a municipal page on lift inspections on her phone. Then she pressed the button. "Eleven, please," she told nobody, and laughed at herself.

qa.q: What did the certificate beside the lift door say?
qa.a: That the lift was inspected last month.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi sit down on the first step?
qa.a: She felt uneasy about climbing eleven floors every day because of one vivid story, and wanted to check how often lifts really fail before changing her habit.

qa.q: What sources did Jahnavi check, and what makes them useful?
qa.a: The inspection certificate, the watchman's twelve years with the lift and a municipal page; together they show how the lift really behaves, not how one story felt.

qa.q: What would change if Jahnavi had simply trusted Noor's voice note?
qa.a: She might have climbed eleven floors with a laptop bag every day, changing her habits because of a story rather than facts.

grounding: A young woman stops herself after a vivid lift story and checks inspection records and local experience before changing her habit.

passage:
"Did you see this?" Anand held out his phone. "A phone blew up on someone's pillow while charging. Look at the burnt sheet."
Usha looked. "That's horrible." She glanced at her own phone charging beside the bed. "Okay. Before I panic, how often does that actually happen?"
"It's everywhere today."
"Everywhere today, sure. How many phones are charging tonight in this city?"
"Lakhs, probably."
"And how many fires like this do we hear about?"
Anand scrolled. "This is the one they're all sharing."
"Let me check the fire service's safety page." She read for a while. "Rare, it says. The ones they see mostly involve cheap chargers, or phones under pillows."
"So?"
"So I'll keep charging it on the table with the proper charger, not under my pillow." She smiled. "And I'll stop scrolling burnt sheets."

qa.q: What did the fire service's safety page say about most such fires?
qa.a: They mostly involve cheap chargers, or phones under pillows.

qa.q: How can you tell Usha felt a flash of worry before checking?
qa.a: She called it horrible and glanced at her own phone charging beside the bed, showing a moment of fear before she chose to check the facts.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking how often it really happens and reading the fire service page led to a small sensible change instead of fear: the proper charger, on the table.

qa.q: What might Anand take away from the conversation?
qa.a: Anand may see that the post felt huge because everyone was sharing it, not because such fires are common.

grounding: A young woman stops at a vivid viral story, asks how often it really happens and reads a reliable source before changing a habit.

passage: Karthik, you called that new boy a nerd because of his glasses, na? Come, sit with your Neelam paati for a minute. When I was ten, in our Madurai school, there were two boys in my row. Venkat wore thick glasses and never spoke, so I was sure he was the class first. Balu shouted jokes all day, so I was sure he was the class last. When I had to choose a partner for the maths competition, I picked Venkat and felt very clever. We came fourth. Balu and his partner won the whole district. Later I found out Venkat loved drawing, not sums, and Balu did maths puzzles every night with his father. I had judged both of them by their covers, and I got both covers wrong.

qa.q: Who won the district maths competition?
qa.a: Balu and his partner.

qa.q: Why did young Neelam feel clever choosing Venkat?
qa.a: She felt confident because his glasses and silence matched her picture of a topper, so he seemed a safe choice.

qa.q: At which point in the story could Neelam have chosen better, and how?
qa.a: When picking a maths partner, she could have looked at who actually solved sums in class, instead of going by glasses and noise.

qa.q: How might Venkat have felt being picked for maths?
qa.a: Venkat might have felt pressured and uneasy, since he loved drawing, not sums, and was chosen for his glasses.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at ten, she assumed a quiet boy with glasses was the topper and a loud boy was weak, and got both wrong.

passage: "Two minutes to pick your quiz partner, captains!" called Madhuri ma'am. Rain was drumming on the tin roof and half the class was absent with flu, so Omkar had only four boys to choose from. He looked fast. Chirag, quiet, round glasses, always reading: surely a genius. Rakesh, who made silly noises during assembly: surely hopeless. "Chirag!" Omkar said. In the quiz, Chirag froze at every buzzer. Rakesh, on the other team, answered six science questions in a row, laughing loudly each time. At the break Omkar muttered, "But he looks like a topper." Chirag heard and shrugged. "I like reading stories, not science." Omkar went red and didn't know where to look.

qa.q: How many questions in a row did Rakesh answer?
qa.a: Six science questions.

qa.q: Why did Omkar go red at the break?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because Chirag heard him say he looked like a topper, and it was clear the glasses had not meant what Omkar thought.

qa.q: What could Omkar try next time he picks a team, even in a hurry?
qa.a: Think of who actually answered well in past science lessons, instead of who looks clever.

qa.q: What is it like for Chirag to be picked for his glasses?
qa.a: Chirag probably felt awkward and under pressure, freezing at the buzzer in a quiz about something he doesn't love.

grounding: In a rushed quiz pick, a boy chooses a quiet classmate with glasses as the genius and writes off a noisy one, who turns out strong.

passage: In the colony clubhouse in Kolkata, the summer chess camp paired players by drawing names. Tanvir drew Arnab, the loud boy who sang film songs on the swings. He grinned. "Easy win." His sister Vandana drew Subho, quiet, thick glasses, a book under his arm. "Bad luck, didi," Tanvir whispered. "He'll finish you." Twenty minutes later Vandana had checkmated Subho, who admitted he only came because his mother made him. Tanvir was still at his board, sweating. Arnab had taken his queen with a knight and was humming while he waited. "How are you so good?" Tanvir asked. "My nani and I play every night," said Arnab. Tanvir stared at the board, then at Arnab's grin, and tried to remember why he'd been so sure.

qa.q: What piece did Arnab take with a knight?
qa.a: Tanvir's queen.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir so sure he would beat Arnab?
qa.a: He felt confident because loud, singing Arnab didn't match his idea of a clever player, while quiet Subho with glasses did.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do before the next camp game?
qa.a: Watch how players actually play, or ask about their practice, instead of judging from glasses or singing.

qa.q: What might Vandana make of Tanvir's warning after her game?
qa.a: She would likely find it funny, since the boy Tanvir said would finish her lost to her in twenty minutes.

grounding: At a chess camp, a boy assumes the quiet boy with glasses is the strong player and the loud singer is weak, and is proved wrong.

passage: At the kasba high school in Nanded district, Irawati's group needed a fourth member for the maths model. "Not her," Irawati whispered, nodding at Kavitha, the new girl from the hill village, who said "ho-ji" to teachers and whose Marathi had a thick village lilt. "She'll be slow. Take Ruchika, she talks like a news reader." Ruchika joined and spent two days making the chart pretty. On the third day, with the model due, their pyramid kept collapsing. Kavitha, walking past with her tiffin, stopped. "Your base angles are wrong. Here." She took a pencil, did the sums in the margin in under a minute, and the pyramid stood. Irawati's mouth hung open. "How did you...?" "My father builds houses," said Kavitha. "Angles are dinner talk."

qa.q: What was wrong with the group's pyramid?
qa.a: Its base angles were wrong, so it kept collapsing.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel so sure Kavitha would be slow?
qa.a: She felt sure and a little superior, because Kavitha's village accent and polite ho-ji matched her picture of a weak student, so the match felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Irawati do next time the group chooses a member?
qa.a: Ask people what they're good at, or look at their actual work, instead of choosing by how they speak.

qa.q: What might it be like for Kavitha to be passed over and then fix the model?
qa.a: Kavitha may have felt left out at first, then calm and quietly proud when her sums made the pyramid stand.

grounding: A teenager judges a new girl as weak at maths from her village accent and is surprised when she solves the problem.

passage: When Mr Duarte announced that each class in their Lisbon school would pick a mentor for the fifth graders' reading club, Beatriz ruled Jamal out at once. Tall, hood always up, earphones in, slang in every sentence: the type who ends up outside the head's office. "He'll scare them," she told her friend, and volunteered herself instead. On Thursday Jamal came along only because the library was warm. Within ten minutes, Beatriz's group of ten-year-olds was fidgeting, and Jamal's was silent, leaning in, as he did the voices of three pirates. One small girl wouldn't let go of his sleeve at the end. "I read to my little brothers every night," he said, shrugging, when Beatriz stared. She walked home turning it over, slightly embarrassed.

qa.q: What did Jamal do to hold the children's attention?
qa.a: He did the voices of three pirates.

qa.q: Why was Beatriz so surprised by Jamal in the library?
qa.a: She was surprised, and a little embarrassed, because his hood, earphones and slang had seemed like proof he was trouble, yet he was the best reader there.

qa.q: What could Beatriz try before ruling someone out next time?
qa.a: Give the person a chance to show what they can do, or ask them, instead of deciding from clothes and slang.

qa.q: How might Jamal feel if he knew why Beatriz ruled him out?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and judged, since he reads to his little brothers every night and was dismissed for his hood and slang.

grounding: A teenager decides a classmate is trouble from his clothes and slang, and is surprised when he is the best reader with young children.

passage: At the district sports hostel in Kottayam, Elizabeth was picking the relay team for the inter-hostel meet. Siddharth, the new boy, was thin, spoke softly and carried a physics book everywhere. "Nerds don't sprint," she said to Coach, and put him down as reserve. Coach only nodded. "Time trials Saturday, then." On Saturday, the stopwatch said what Elizabeth didn't want to hear: Siddharth ran the hundred faster than two of her chosen runners, and his baton change was the cleanest on the track. She looked at her list, then at him, retying his laces as if it was nothing. "Why didn't you say?" she asked. "You didn't ask," he said, not unkindly. She tore up the list and wrote a new one from the times.

qa.q: What did the time trials show about Siddharth?
qa.a: He ran the hundred faster than two of her chosen runners, with the cleanest baton change on the track.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth put Siddharth down as reserve?
qa.a: She felt sure a thin, soft-spoken boy with a physics book could not sprint, so matching him to a type felt like enough evidence.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, and why?
qa.a: The time trials, because they judged every runner on real speed instead of on how they looked.

qa.q: How might Siddharth have felt being put down as reserve?
qa.a: He may have felt quietly overlooked but calm, trusting the stopwatch to show what he could do.

grounding: A teen captain assumes a quiet boy with a physics book cannot sprint and is surprised when the time trials say otherwise.

passage:
12 October, hostel room, late
Survey deadline today. Guess who delivered? Not Manoj.
Three weeks ago I voted for him as group leader without thinking twice. He gave that speech in the first class without notes, sounded like someone on a TV panel, used words like "synergy" and made everyone laugh. Bindu didn't even raise her hand. She just sat there with her colour-coded planner.
Today Manoj had "a few directions we could explore" and no survey. Bindu had quietly made the whole questionnaire, tested it on her roommates and uploaded it at 6 a.m. Nobody asked her to.
I voted in about three seconds, just from how he talks. I still like listening to him. I just don't think I'd trust him with a deadline again.
Rekha

qa.q: What time did Bindu upload the questionnaire?
qa.a: At 6 a.m.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling about the vote now?
qa.a: Rekha feels frustrated and a bit foolish for voting in three seconds because of Manoj's smooth speech, while still enjoying listening to him.

qa.q: What could the group look at next time it picks a leader?
qa.a: Who plans the work and meets small deadlines, like Bindu with her planner and tested questionnaire, rather than who gives the best speech.

qa.q: How might Bindu feel doing the work without being chosen?
qa.a: Bindu might feel unnoticed or taken for granted, since she did the survey unasked while Manoj got the title.

grounding: A student's diary shows choosing a fluent, confident speaker as leader and overlooking a quieter, more reliable teammate.

passage: The NSS camp in a village near Kolar had one job for the week: map every household's water source. Maria, the group coordinator, needed a team lead. Ramesh stood up in the panchayat hall and spoke to the sarpanch like a politician, full of big words about development. "He's our man," Maria wrote in her notebook on the spot. Pallavi, who had quietly asked for a village map on the first day, was given the job of carrying water bottles. By Wednesday Ramesh had given two more speeches and visited nine houses. Pallavi, on her own evening walks, had marked all eighty-four wells and taps on the map in blue ink. When the professor asked for the survey, it was Pallavi's map that Maria handed over, red-faced.

qa.q: How many wells and taps did Pallavi mark?
qa.a: Eighty-four, in blue ink.

qa.q: Why was Maria red-faced handing over Pallavi's map?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, because she had picked Ramesh for his confident speeches and given Pallavi, who did the real work, the water bottles.

qa.q: What went wrong in choosing the lead, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Maria chose by speaking style; next time she could give a small task first and see who plans and finishes it, as Pallavi did with the map.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about being handed the water bottles?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt overlooked and a little hurt, yet she kept going and quietly finished the survey anyway.

passage: The hiring panel at the hospital's IT department had seen six candidates by lunch. Abhinav was excited about the fourth. "He's another Rakesh. Same college, same cricket-club style, even the same laugh. Rakesh turned out brilliant." The third panellist agreed. Hemant, running a panel for the first time, looked at his notes. The fifth candidate, a woman from a small polytechnic, had solved the database problem fastest and explained it most clearly. Nobody had mentioned her. "Can I suggest something?" Hemant said. "Let's each score all six on the same four points: the problem, the explanation, the teamwork answer and learning. Out of five. Before we talk." Abhinav grumbled but filled in the sheet. When the scores were added, the fifth candidate was first, and Rakesh's lookalike was fourth.

qa.q: How many candidates had the panel seen by lunch?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why did Hemant suggest scoring before talking?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that the panel was drawn to a candidate who resembled Rakesh while nobody mentioned the candidate who had solved the problem best.

qa.q: Why does scoring all six on the same four points help?
qa.a: It makes each panellist judge every candidate on the same evidence before excitement about a lookalike can sway the room.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel when the scores are added?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel surprised and a little embarrassed that the lookalike he liked came fourth.

grounding: A young manager notices his panel favouring a candidate who resembles a past success and proposes scoring everyone on the same points.

Subject: Proposal for next week's interview panels
Hi Sabina,
After sitting on three panels for the analyst roles, I want to flag something. Last year's best hire came from Pune and played football, and since then we keep rating candidates higher when they share those things. On Tuesday one candidate got "strong fit" from two panellists mainly because "he reminds us of Kunal." Another candidate, who answered the case question best, got "not sure about culture."

Yash

passage: Ganga, the story I tell new managers is from my first hiring panel, when I was the only man under thirty in the room. We were choosing trainee chefs for the hotel kitchen. The head chef kept lighting up at candidates who had trained where he had, spoke like him, even stood like him. "This one has the look," he'd say. A young woman from a small catering college cooked the best omelette of the day, and he said, "Not the type." I was scared to contradict him. So I didn't argue about her. I said, "Chef, can we taste blind for the next round? Numbers on the plates, scores on a sheet, names after?" He shrugged and agreed. She came first. Dhruv, the nervous junior, got to feel useful that day.

qa.q: What did the young woman from the catering college cook?
qa.a: The best omelette of the day.

qa.q: How was Dhruv feeling about speaking up?
qa.a: Dhruv was scared to contradict the head chef, so chose a neutral method instead of arguing about one candidate.

qa.q: Why did the blind tasting work better than arguing?
qa.a: It judged every candidate on the food itself, so looks and training background could not sway the scores.

qa.q: How might the head chef see the blind-tasting result?
qa.a: He may be surprised that the candidate he called not the type came first, and it could make him question his instinct for the look.

grounding: A young man on a hiring panel notices the head chef favouring candidates like himself and proposes blind, scored tasting.
